To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) fails for spherocylinder cells and that the modified Pearson correlation coefficient (MPCC) corrects this failure.
the Pearson Correlation coefficient (PCC) fails to correctly measure the degree of linear spatial correlation between 2D projections from two different proteins in spherocylinder cells.

the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) systematically underestimates both the degree of anti-correlation between the 2D projections and the degree of correlation between 3D distributions for spherocylinder cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new statistical tools for analysis of spatial distributions in live bacterial cells.
the analysis of two color fluorescence microscopy images.
a new statistical method to quantify the degree of correlation between two differently labeled protein distributions within the same live cell, in the case of spheroidal cell shapes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Pearson correlation coefficient is not a good statistic for assessing the linear correlation of two differently colored images in spherocytindrical cells.
the MPCC is an improved measure of linear correlation for two color imaging of spherocylinder cells.

PCC should not be used to assess linear correlation between the projections onto the camera plane of 3D distributions of fluorescence intensity in spherocylinder shaped cells, and that MPCC should be used instead.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MPCC provides a quantitative and robust measure for the degree of correlation between two differently labeled proteins within a spherocylindrically shaped cell.
the PCC is a poor statistic for comparing the linear correlation between two distributions in 3D sphericylindrical cells.
PCC is inappropriate for 2D projection of 3D distributions of proteins in spherocylinder cells and should not be used.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Pearson Correlation statistic is not appropriate for analysis of two color images of 3D distributions in cells with non spherical geometry.

the Pearson Correlation coefficient should be used with great caution when analyzing the spatial distributions of two different species in 3D sphericylindrical cells, and should be replaced with the MPCC for this special case.
the PCC should not be used to assess the correlation of two differently labeled protein distributions in spherocytindrical cells.
